title: Stopping Distances & Keeping Back
whatItIs: Large vehicles need a greater distance to stop. Never get closer than your overall stopping distance: keep at least a two-second gap, four seconds in a tunnel, and far more on wet or icy roads.
keyFacts: Drive at a speed that lets you stop well within the distance you can see to be clear.
Never get closer to the vehicle in front than your overall stopping distance.
Keep at least a two-second gap on high-speed roads and in tunnels. Large vehicles need a greater distance to stop.
Driving a large vehicle in a tunnel: allow a four-second gap. If you stop in a tunnel, leave at least 5 metres.
Wet roads: stopping distances at least double. Icy roads: they can be ten times greater.
If someone overtakes and pulls into the gap in front of you, drop back to restore a two-second gap.

onTheTest.question: You're driving a lorry through a road tunnel. What gap should you leave to the vehicle in front?
onTheTest.why: Large vehicles need a greater distance to stop. If you are driving a large vehicle in a tunnel, you should allow a four-second gap.

onTheTest.question: The road is wet. How should your following gap change?
options: Reduce it, as traffic is slower
onTheTest.why: In wet weather, stopping distances will be at least double those on dry roads, so the gap should be at least doubled.

traps: In a tunnel: four seconds while moving, but at least 5 metres when stopped. Don’t mix them up.
ABS keeps you steering, but don't assume it will stop you in a shorter distance.
Ice can make stopping distances ten times greater, not just double.
In fog, rear lights ahead can give a false sense of security: keep a safe distance.
